rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Sabaʾ lived in what is now Yemen, a fertile, lush region with orchards along its main highway and throughout its territory.
rows.anchor: They inhabited the area now called Yemen. It was a very fertile and lush land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite the abundant land and orchards, the people of Sabaʾ failed to value God’s blessing; their ingratitude was punished by a flood that destroyed their country.
rows.anchor: However, these people did not give due regard to this blessing of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grateful David and Solomon were presented earlier; Sabaʾ now illustrates the fate of the ungrateful, and Quraysh are also directed to learn from its fate in verses 112–113.
rows.anchor: Earlier, the characters of David (sws) and Solomon (sws) were presented as grateful servants of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabāʾ refers here to the people of Sabaʾ.
rows.anchor: The word إَِبَس refers to the people of Sabā’.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word maskan here means “territory” or “land.”
rows.anchor: The word ِنَكْسَم here means “territory” or “land.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form of āyah, without alif lām, conveys the sign’s majesty and magnitude: it testified to God’s mercy, providence, and favors.
rows.anchor: The word ٌةَیآ is not defined by an alif lām to portray its majesty and magnitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabaʾ’s sign was a central highway bordered on both sides by a succession of orchards.
rows.anchor: a series of orchards existed on both their both sides ie left and right.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dual jannatān means two rows of orchards, not merely two individual gardens; Arabic uses dual nouns this way when context supports it.
rows.anchor: The word ِانَتَّنَج here does not mean two “orchards.” It means “two lines of orchards.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gardens’ visible prosperity itself calls people to benefit from God’s provision and show gratitude.
rows.anchor: These manifestations of advancement and grandeur by their very existence are calling out that people should benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṭayyibah means “lush and fertile,” a sense used in many Qur’anic passages.
rows.anchor: means “lush and fertile.” It is used in this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abundant provision shows that the Lord is forgiving and merciful: He richly provided even an undeserving, ungrateful people.
rows.anchor: in spite of their ungratefulness He has richly provided them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude to a benefactor is an obvious requirement of human nature; someone without this awareness is worse than an animal.
rows.anchor: expressing gratitude to someone who confers favours and blessings is an obvious requirement of human nature.

rows.speaker: Some lexicographers
rows.claim: Some lexicographers understand ʿarim to mean “pounding rain.”
rows.anchor: Some lexicographers are of the opinion that the word ِمِرَع means “pounding rain”

rows.speaker: Other lexicographers
rows.claim: Other lexicographers say ʿarim is the plural of ʿarimah, stones piled in layers; the term then came to mean a valley structure or bulwark that stops water.
rows.anchor: others say that it is the plural of عَرِمَة which refers to stones gathered in many layers one over the other.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi adopts the dam sense, citing Aqrab al-mawārid’s definition of a dam built in a valley and the historic Sabaʾ dam; Mangla and Tarbela are comparable examples.
rows.anchor: Mangla and Tarbela dams are its examples in Pakistan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Sabaʾ had the long, wide Maʿārib dam, which protected them from floods and irrigated their lands; it stood by their capital, Maʿārib, and probably failed around 542 CE, destroying the country.
rows.anchor: It is named Sadd-i Ma‘ārib. Ma‘ārib was the capital of Sabā’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After God’s favor, Sabaʾ grew arrogant and ignored a warning messenger; a great flood then destroyed the dam and devastated the land.
rows.anchor: the Almighty sent a messenger to them to warn them but they showed indifference to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khamṭ means bitter and bad-tasting; the flood replaced the luxuriant gardens with bitter-fruited trees and lotus bushes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flood deposited mud or sand that changed the remaining vegetation, leaving wild bushes and shrubs across the land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words attributed to Sabaʾ portray the attitude their existence expressed: they deserved ruined settlements, difficult journeys, and confiscated favors.
rows.anchor: These words are not uttered by them; they in fact portray what emanates from their very existence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their request to be distanced from journeys is a portrayal of their situation, not an actual utterance; Islahi says the Qur’an similarly portrays the Jews’ words in 2:93.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their ingratitude and disobedience wronged their own souls and brought God’s wrath; they could not harm God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being made a tale of the ancients describes the consequence of their ingratitude: they were routed and ravaged.
